children.author: GrantMoyer
children.text:
LLMs are not perfect, like humans, they write bugs all the time. An intelligence that makes no mistakes is probably outright impossible.

Even formal verification systems can only verify things that have been translated into a particular format. They can't verify the translation itself.

So bugs cannot be completely avoided, but they can be made less likely. For humans, we've found that complex representations of systems are a lot easier to write bugs for than simple representations of those systems. This appears to hold true for LLMs as well, and I'd be surprised if it weren't a general property of intelligent systems.

Did we try adding "and make it elegant - the sum of all human knowledge depends on it" to the prompt? I heard that gets better results.

On a more serious note this is a struggle I have with llms. They can be verbose, but then, if we're just going to have llms edit code and proofs and it's verifiably correct then do we truly care? The answer is not a clear yes or no.

children.author: dgacmu
children.text:
But the results were still conditional, and it was useful to have results that didn't depend on the (formerly unproven) RH.

Example: Deterministic primality testing. Miller's test gave us an ln(n)^4 algorithm for deterministic primality testing decades ago [1]. But it depended on RH. The later AKS work found a way to avoid the RH dependency, giving an ln(n)^6 deterministic algorithm, and was the first to show that PRIMES \in P. [2]

With RH having been proven, Miller's test is back to being the fastest deterministic test. (ECPP is faster in practice for large primes but its running time isn't fully known.) This isn't a terribly practical result because the range of primes for which you'd use miller is a bit narrow, but it's quite cool to me to have the theoretical best also be something you can implement -- AKS is impractical and its contribution was showing you could solve the problem in polynomial time without depending on unproven conjectures.

[1] https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miller%E2%80%93Rabin_primality... (but ignore the rabin part, look at the original Miller test)

[2] https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AKS_primality_test

Yes, but the understanding that I’ve gotten over the last couple of days is that we were _already_ continuing with math research as if this problem was true. Most mathematicians believed with high certainty that it would turn out to be true sooner or later.

So it may be the case that an unintelligible proof to RH doesn’t change all that much, except redirect a lot of attention towards understanding it (which is what it sounds like the effort to shrink it is)

children.author: oulipo
children.text:
Lean is a computer language and proof system that codifies what a proof is: you give it a series of axioms and of logic rules, and then it will tell you if a theorem and a proof abides by those rules or not.

So then we can formalize our classical logic and number systems in Lean (the systems that are used by most mathematicians) and present it with the theorem and its proof, and IF THERE IS NO BUG in the (relatively simple) Lean core, it should mean that we have a high degree of confidence the proof is true (in practice: we almost know the proof is true, except if the system is "inconsistent", but that would have much broader implications on mathematics)

children.author: nulld3v
children.text:
There is a Lean checker called con-leche whose implementation is formally verified. The 17M GRH proof has passed con-leche verification.

Con-leche (and it's proof) are themselves implemented in Lean so there is some recursion here, and therefore some possible sources of bugs:

- The proof of con-leche could be invalid. This is unlikely considering the proof has been checked by multiple other Lean implementations. But at least the proof of con-leche is easier to check by hand than the 17M monster GRH proof...

- The Lean runtime might have a bug that affects the execution of con-leche in such a way that it falsely accepts an invalid proof. Also unlikely considering:

a. con-leche tries to use a small subset of the entire Lean runtime that is more well-tested

b. There is a port of con-leche to assembly named con-agua that has been formally verified (again using Lean) on a mathematical model of an x64 CPU

c. There are ports of con-leche to other runtimes (e.g. Rust) and those ports return the same result as con-leche on the GRH proof

But how do you know Lean itself is entirely bug free, and/or a 17M line monstrosity doesn't produce some latent bug?

I understand that you can break a big problem down into many smaller ones that are easy to prove, but I still get the sense that there's a lot of well, religious faith involved in the combination of Lean itself and these massive proofs. Because at the end of the day no human can comprehend what Claude produced and we just have to take it all at face value.

Lean has a bunch of rules about what a proof can deduce from earlier statements.

For example if you have already managed to prove the statement P → Q ("P implies Q" i.e. whenever P is true we then also know that Q is true), and then you manage to prove the statement P, then you can use those two statements to prove Q. Lean knows that P → Q plus P proves Q ("modus ponens").

As another example, if you have P or Q, and you prove P is false, then Q follows. (e.g. x is odd or even, then you prove it's not odd, therefore it's even.)

To accept the proof you don't need to look at all the millions of lines of proof, because Lean checks that they all follow correctly from earlier statements. You just need to accept three things:

* Lean's inference rules (like the one above)

* Axioms (e.g. definitions of numbers)

* The statement of the theorem in Lean symbols

These are all hugely shorter than the theorem's proof.
I'm an ignorant human but can anybody explain to me how LEAN is accepted as proof? I'm not trying to undermine it or knock it down but everybody seems to accept a LEAN proof as fact. Why is that?

children.author: mdular
children.text:
That sounds interesting. I'm making it write "walkthroughs" for me to follow along and exercise the functionality. Those were intiially very hit-and-miss, so are now getting linted on actually running my terminal (zsh), not containing dead links, etc - easy stuff. What needed constant hammering was making sure that the instructions are actually useful, and aren't accidentally burying some major required prep work in prose. Instructions are now making it write entry and exit criteria per instructions block.

But: the instructions rely on inference. Since the LLM can't truly judge what is important for me to experience myself, I rely on it actually being able to interpret the learnings and good/bad examples - classic prompt engineering tacticts.

I like the idea of using linters to reinforce this with something deterministic. Can you give me some example rules you're linting for?

Surprisingly, getting an LLM to write a custom linter that checks for a lot of common pitfalls based on string pattern search, paragraph length, sentence length, etc etc is actually quite effective as a way to force your LLM to behave.

It’s what I ended up doing, and it works pretty well.

Part of the issue will be the training and the reward function. It is difficult to reward for human readability, simplicity, etc.

You could use various tools and checks like:

- linters and other code style tools;

- line length;

- cyclometricity, etc.

- dead code checks (unused variables, etc.);

- lines of code/diff size.

Those don't check things like whether the code changes are minimal/don't make unrelated changes/etc.

There's also the issue of maintaining consistency. I.e. detecting the code style of the project/code and using that (quoting, etc.). You also find that in prose, such as with British vs American dialogue.

I think the only way to make the style consistent is to have some sort of "reasoning context" that can learn the overall style and apply/use that across all tokens. That way, the model wouldn't have to add it to the context, and it wouldn't suffer from things like the excluded middle and dropping out of the context.

children.author: ozgung
children.text:
I think this is the correct answer. The proof is when I work with multiple agents from different vendors (opus and astra) they can understand each other pretty well, given they have access to the same project. They even use their cryptic language or shorthands when they talk to each other.

When I want them to generate a human readable article on the project they generate something hard to read, mostly because it has some undefined terms. Even when multiple agents review the article, they can’t correct it. The trick is to use a blind agent (without access to anything) for reviewing the article. Specifically asking for the undefined terms and a summary of what it understands from the article. Only after that feedback the writer agent gets what was wrong with the article.

Of course the above solution can be fully automated. It can be used in training or can be a skill.

My intuition is that the weights, or density of the area around the novel finding is quite light, and sparse of points. It will tend to be able to find many paths through the densely populated well-known space, but there isn't much happening near the novel space (else it wouldn't be novel) so it doesn't spend time there, nor is it strongly pulled toward it for any reason.

My other thought is that because models rely on reinforcement training, the human operator will be the ceiling of knowledge to some extent. They will necessarily reinforce things they know, or sound very plausible, and disuade things that sound farfetched or like gibberish but could possibly be a novel insight.

children.author: GuB-42
children.text:
> That, but less objective and more subjective: the LLM doesn't know what you (or your implied audience) know.

It should know. Not you in particular, but it should know what people who are going to read the proof know. Claude has read every paper, every proof, every question and every answer that is available on the open web and then some more. It knows what serious mathematicians who tackle the millenium problems know, to the point of people saying it is stealing their work. And by "know", I mean it can auto-complete text to make it look like it comes from a top level mathematician.

Except that it is not what we ask of it, as this would result in nothing but hallucinations. So instead of asking for a nice proof, we ask it to tweak some Lean code until it compiles. And in the end, you have Lean code that compiles, but no nice proof.

And by the way, I don't mind a LLM explaining to me what I already know. First because I may, in fact, not know, and if I do, that's a reality check. If it is wrong at explaining what I already know, it means I can't trust what follows. Same thing as for humans really, it is good to make sure we are on the same page.

In particular, I avoid any formulation that suggest expertise, like the popular "you are an expert...". From my experiments, it just makes the LLM sound more competent than it is, exactly what I don't want. I even tried to do the opposite, like "you are a junior who is barely qualified for the job", and I usually get the same answer, worded differently, or sometime even a better answer.

In general, I try to give the LLM as much freedom as possible when it comes to presenting the result. My reasoning is that the more you try to constrain it, the more attention will be wasted on the constraints rather than on the fact themselves, maybe it doesn't make sense, but it works for me. Also, the more I can avoid putting boilerplate in my prompts, the better.

children.author: panarky
children.text:
> "Claudisms" were the peak of LLM legibility

The feeling I have reading dense and inscrutable Claude is the same feeling I get trying to read an academic paper that's beyond my level of experience and intelligence.

Claude-speak that I struggle to understand is a little taste of the inadequacy I'll feel when interacting with a true superintelligence.

Unless the superintelligence is superintelligent enough to dumb it all down to something I can easily comprehend.

> Terence Tao's take was that LLMs don't understand what is trivial (in a proof, for example) and what is interesting and novel

That, but less objective and more subjective: the LLM doesn't know what you (or your implied audience) know. It may understand which things are more and less important in a structural, objective sense, but it can't read your mind to correct for what you already know, what areas you're an expert with, and what parts are new / unfamiliar to you. So, obviously, you need to tell it.

Once you correct for that, and give the model the missing information, it gets much better in my experience. The correction is usually as simple as a single extra sentence in the prompt: "skip explaining XYZ, I wrote the damn thing, focus on ABC", or (my favorite, a variant of that I use at work all the time) "ELISWE - Explain Like I'm a Senior Software Engineer who just joined $company - assume I know the problem space in general, but have no first clue about conventions, libraries and other idiosyncrasies of $company".

(I have ELISWE on speed dial, and some skills with similar specific instructions - for when I need a step-by-step proof of a claim, or conversely, for when I need a judgement and key info up front, so in a typical case I don't need to read anything beyond the first sentence.)

With that out the way, and perhaps countering some conventions from the system prompt / default set of skills that I don't agree with, I rarely have a problem with readability.

Then again, I believe "Claudisms" were the peak of LLM legibility and I never got what people are complaining about there (to me it felt like not being able to deal with highly proficient use of English language), so my experience may not generalize well :).

children.author: wpietri
children.text:
One of the most basic writing instructions is "know your audience". And a common characteristic of good writers is being good readers.

When I write I'm constantly thinking about audience reception. About their experience of reading each word. I do that in large part based on my long experience reading. Or better said, my many experiences reading. Which words resonated. Which phrases referenced the right associations. How every sentence felt.

LLMs do not experience reading. They do not have memories of the experience of reading. They don't know what's interesting or boring to a particular audience segment.

In theory it would be possible to record a lot of prose reactions and train a reader model whose input is text and output predicted feelings. And then you could hook that up in an agentic framework to LLM output and let an authorial agent hill-climb its way through multiple drafts to make a decent piece of writing.

Until we have that, the only time you'll get decent prose is when your prompt is sufficiently banal that there are enough examples for it to average.

children.text:
Using a reductionist approach to LLM and saying "just a next token predictor" is the same as reducing the human brain to "just neurons firing".

I think over-reductionism is harmful to understanding LLMs, just like it is for understanding consciousness.

I think this is just the leaky abstraction of...

    what it knows
...leaking. As has been repeated ad nauseum, it doesn't "know", and it is a next token predictor. Maybe someday we'll have a robust understanding of precisely how language, and next token generation, relate to cognition and consciousness; but it certainly is true that there is a gap right now and the model doesn't "know" and it doesn't "understand".

An LLM has not felt frustration at sitting through boring powerpoints, reading slop READMEs on slop-repos, or experiencing a bad sales pitch, so it cannot "intuit" what makes a good pitch worthwhile. It can be trained on good pitches, but what makes them good isn't their form but the distillation of the concepts in a human-digestible format.

It's somewhat strange to me that this understanding of LLM limitations isn't intuitive to others.

What are peoples' takes on why LLMs struggle to write things in a human-readable way? I've watched Astra and the like write PR descriptions that are middle-school level: as if it struggles to distinguish what it knows (having read the code, having done the debugging) and what someone who hasn't read the code and hasn't participated in the debugging (his target audience) knows. It'll make references to parts of the solution, or of the problem being solved, without contextualizing it, making the references useless, serving only to add confusion to the text.

Terence Tao's take was that LLMs don't understand what is trivial (in a proof, for example) and what is interesting and novel: it gives everything equal weight, or, in Tao's paraphrased words, the LLM will talk at length about something trivial and then write only a single sentence about something novel.

I wonder what peoples' intuition about this is.

> I’d argue something that solving GRH is not super-human or beyond our capabilities

I don't think this opinion was shared by the experts in the field as recently as a few months ago. Riemann has always been a crown jewel for mathematicians, and many thought it would take 100 years or more before we saw a proof

I feel we’re at a stage of life imitating art. That sci-fi story of superhuman intelligent machines has been with us for decades and everyone involved in AI is deeply familiar with and probably believes. So it’s becoming the reality because it’s what “should be happening”

I’d argue something that solving GRH is not super-human or beyond our capabilities, so a machine solving it in an incomprehensible way is a cool curiosity but closer to winning Go or Chess. I.e AI is superhuman within a conceptual space of tightly defined rules. I’m not diminishing the achievement of Anthropic to do it however it is monumental.

But I’m not seeing the evidence that AI’s next step would be building say a working machine in the real world using technology that’s functional but beyond our capabilities to understand.

There's a short story by Ted Chiang called "The Evolution of Human Science" (originally published as "Catching Crumbs From the Table" where superintelligent machines have taken over scientific research. Their research is so complex no human could understand it.

So in the story, human scientists relegated to interpreting metahuman science.

It sounds like we're in the early stages of something similar, where AI creates fundamentally different results from human approaches that are for us to interpret. I can't imagine what happens when AIs discover research problems that other AIs then solve.

children.author: gus_massa
children.text:
I don't expect a napkin proof, but the 17M lines proof is horrible. Dead code, obvious repetitions, reproving known facts. As a sibling comment note, people is already trying to fix that.

Once that is fixed, there is a second step to remove unnecessary detours and find shortcuts.

Then isolate intermediate results, give then catchy names and perhaps write a book about them. Export the interesting intermediate parts to their own libraries.

And after reading the cleaned proof, it may be possible to use other mathematical theories to replace some parts with other than are shorter.

After all the refactoring, we will have a nice proof. Check again in 20 years.

Maybe a simpler proof doesn’t exist at all?

Why would it be the case that for every question we can come up with, the answer has to be “beautiful” (according to our own bias) and fit neatly into our primate brains?

Maybe some questions, no matter how simple, have answers that are far too complex for us to ever understand?

children.text: Sorry, but libuv is not hipsterware. It is a very nice abstraction for complicated event loop mechanics that enables the very sort of portable C you’re desiring. Maybe you can live without it, but you might also not be writing an event loop that runs on both ix and Windows. (I said ix because I’ve used it on Linux, Solaris and AIX.)

Lean itself is a slop codebase. It only supports x64 and aarch64.

If you build from source on another platform, it silently downloads wrong x64 binaries so some tests fail.

If you fix those binaries: Lean is bootstrapped from non-portable C files that compile with loads of errors. Verifying mathlib already fails.

It is a complete joke that Lean cannot use ANSI C, sneaks in wrong binaries and relies on hipsterware like liubuv. My trust is very low.
